exclude: Generated VIC matrix and sprite pointers. The copy loop at $1D81 fills the first 1016 bytes, and $1A25–$1A48 sets the last eight.
Generated bitmap. $1DC9 first clears the destination and $091C reveals the pixels from the stored bitmap. The running capture matches the corresponding source range byte for byte.
Carried from the previous part, byte-identical before load, at entry and at the running screen. CPU fetch, read and write watches were silent for 160 frames after entry.
Carried from the previous part, byte-identical before load, at entry and at the running screen. CPU fetch, read and write watches were silent for 160 frames after entry.
Opening screen RAM carried into the interlude. The load left the underlying RAM unchanged. The disk prompt clears these sprite slots with I/O banked out before drawing glyphs.
Opening screen RAM carried into the interlude. No underlying RAM writes on the transition. The bytes match the selector, interlude entry and illustrated screen captures.
Opening screen RAM carried into the interlude. No underlying RAM writes on the transition. The colour copy at $1DA5 accesses the colour RAM chip with I/O visible.
RAM inherited from Opening. The load write map shows no writes to this range, and the bytes match before the load, at hand-over and on the displayed screen.

comments.text: 6510 port data direction controlling which bits drive the bank selects.
Processor port that selects ROM, I/O or underlying RAM for the copies and loader calls.
Beginning of the low-page scratch range cleared on exit. The IRQ saves state in its first byte.
Low byte of the current copy or draw pointer. The two-row text renderer also uses it for the lower glyph cell.
Upper byte of the pointer at $04. The page-copy routine decrements it when moving to another page.
The interrupt installer clears this byte at $193C before setting the first raster compare.
Low byte of the upper screen-row pointer in the loading text routine.
High byte of the upper screen-row pointer, formed from the row offset and base page $AC.
Low byte of the upper text row’s colour RAM pointer. The disk-side prompt reuses it for the sprite bitmap destination pointer.
Upper byte of the colour RAM pointer, formed by combining the low page bits with $D8.
Low byte of the colour RAM pointer for the lower glyph row.
Upper page of the lower text colour row in the colour RAM window.
Low byte of the localized loading-script pointer. The bitmap reveal reuses this byte for the selected two-bit pixel mask.
High byte of the loading script pointer, fetched from the odd bytes of its directory.
Index into the dissolve permutation. The routine increments it after applying one pair across the picture.
Cursor into the selected loading text script. The renderer advances it after every glyph.
Counts the picture groups remaining for the current mask in the dissolve loop.
KERNAL output control byte cleared before starting an interlude disk load.
Low byte used for the indirect fetch from a voice’s current track list.
Upper byte of the indirect track-list fetch pointer.
Low address byte used by the voice’s indirect pattern event fetch.
High address byte paired with the pattern pointer low byte at $FE.
Low byte of the KERNAL software IRQ vector. The reset installer changes it with the adjacent high byte.
High byte of the IRQ vector installed alongside $0314.
Page cleared by the interlude reset loop and used for the copied sound driver and transition state during a quest.
Carried disk marker checked before the illustrated interlude proceeds.
Carried loader and side state in the tail of page seven. The interlude writes a marker before transferring to the next load.
Requests the world-specific B file through KERNAL LOAD, relocates the resulting pages, then requests the A file and pushes $0811 so LOAD transfers control to $0812 when it returns.
Contains the side string, the three-character B and A filenames with lengths, and the synthetic LOAD return address minus one.
Length byte followed by the three PETSCII bytes for this world’s A file.
Length supplied to SETNAM when requesting the A file after relocating the B data.
Low byte of the synthetic LOAD return. The loader pushes it after the high byte at $0886.
High byte of the synthetic return from the A load. The CPU returns to $0812.
With I/O banked out, copies pages backward from $C700 to $FF00 and downward, advancing both high bytes an extra two at the $C9 boundary before continuing.
Zero permits the source pixel pair to merge into the destination. A nonzero value takes the clearing branch.

Reveals the $E000 bitmap from $1DE3. Each permutation byte chooses one pixel-pair mask and one offset within a $30-byte stride. The loop at $091C merges that pair into $A7 destination bytes at that stride. A nonzero $08DA skips the writes.
Four masks select one two-bit multicolour pixel in a byte, in the stored order $C0, $0C, $30, $03.
A permutation of $00 through $FF. Its low two bits choose a pixel-pair mask and its upper six bits give the byte offset for one reveal pass.

Selects VIC bank $8000, matrix at $AC00 and charset at $B000. Fills colour RAM, then uses the language index at $C902 to select a positioned script. Converts each glyph to two character cells and writes both cells and their colours.
Three little-endian pointers to the English, German and Italian loading text scripts.
High-byte origin for the loading script pointer lookup. The routine indexes it by twice the selected language.
Loading script with two position-prefixed segments. It places “ELVIRAS MAGICAL QUEENDOM” at row 1, column 8 and “LOADING PLEASE WAIT” at row 5, column 10.
Loading script with two position-prefixed segments. It places “ELVIRAS ZAUBERREICH” at row 1, column 10 and “LADE, BITTE WARTEN” at row 5, column 11.
Loading script with two position-prefixed segments. It places “REGNO MAGICO DI ELVIRA” at row 1, column 9 and “STO CARICANDO, ATTENDI PREGO” at row 5, column 5.
Low-byte origin of the 16-bit row offsets. The script row is multiplied by four so the two glyph rows are consecutive.
High-byte origin in the screen row offset table. $0AB1 reads it with a four-byte stride because each script row occupies two physical rows.
Sets the border, stops CIA 1 timer A, enables the raster IRQ and points the software IRQ vector to $0C20.

Acknowledges the raster IRQ. Alternates between updating the sound player inside a short border colour change and clearing the phase flag. Schedules line $82 before continuing through the KERNAL handler.
Song selection or transition command. The player services the command before the update for each voice.
Enables volume decay when set. The decay helper clears it when the song enters its stop state.
Ticks remaining before the next master-volume decrement. The fade helper reloads it after it expires.
Main update interval counter. While nonzero the tick bypasses pattern advance and only applies voice effects.
Reload value copied into the tick countdown at the end of the voice loop.
Cursor for each voice’s track list. It advances after a pattern ends and returns to zero at the track loop.
Offset of the next byte in the selected pattern for each voice. The player resets it when advancing to a new pattern.
Duration counter for the playing event. New notes and the wait command can reload it.
Configured note duration for each voice. On a note event the player copies it to the active duration counter.
Effect countdown decremented during an active event and tested before applying the frequency sweep.
Value copied into the effect countdown when a note starts.
First instrument modulation parameter. The note trigger uses it to construct the upper and lower frequency limits.
Second instrument modulation parameter. The frequency sweep adds or subtracts it from the active frequency.
Low byte of the upper pitch limit. The sweep compares it with the changing low frequency byte.
High byte of the upper pitch limit. The upper-bound subtraction propagates the low-byte borrow into this byte.
Low byte of the lower pitch limit. The downward sweep compares the active frequency against this value.
High byte of the lower pitch limit, used with the associated low-byte subtraction.
Scratch byte for calculating song and instrument offsets and for saving the current pattern cursor.
SID register offset for the current voice. The player loads it before processing the voice’s events.
Current voice table index, saved before the pattern and instrument dispatches reuse X.
Three SID offsets $00, $07 and $0E for the start of each voice’s register group.
Lower byte of each channel’s track-list address. The player loads it into the indirect track pointer.
Upper byte of each channel’s track-list address. The player fetches it alongside the low-byte table.
Instrument flags for each voice. The effect path copies the current byte and shifts its enable bits in turn.
Flags for the ongoing pitch and pulse-width effects, including their sweep directions.
Shared mode byte. Its low bit enables the alternating filter-cutoff update.
Current voice’s instrument flags, copied to this byte because each effect dispatch shifts out one bit.
Master-volume and filter-mode bits sent to $D418. The fade helper decrements the stored value.
Filter cutoff high byte used by the shared filter update. The player and extended commands can replace it.
The active note number from the pattern, used for the initial frequency and as the base of a relative note offset.
Variable low byte of each voice’s frequency, written to the SID after the modulation update.
Active pulse low byte. Instrument setup stores an initial value and the effect loop modifies it before the SID write.
Per-voice pulse low byte copied into the active pulse state when the note-reset flag is set.
Active pulse width high byte written to SID after adjusting its frequency and pulse effects.
Per-voice pulse high byte restored with the low byte when the note-reset flag is set.
The upper half of the active 16-bit frequency and the last value sent to SID’s frequency high register for this voice.
Unmodified frequency high byte saved at the note trigger. The alternating effect can restore it.
Unmodified frequency low byte saved at note trigger and restored by the alternating effect.
Per-voice addition or subtraction for the pulse-width sweep, updated by an extended note command.
Initial waveform and gate byte from the instrument, used when starting the note and when restoring its original waveform.
Alternate waveform or gate byte. The voice effect path can write it after the note starts.
Per-voice shift byte that delays the follow-up control write until its relevant bit clears.
Temporary adjustment added to the low frequency byte after the pitch-effect timer expires.
Temporary adjustment subtracted from the low frequency byte after the pitch-effect timer expires.
Counter reloaded by the relative pitch commands and decremented while the timed note is playing.
Cursor in the relative note stream. The player advances it after reading an offset and resets it on the loop marker.
Offset used when starting a note or when the relative note stream loops at $80.
Relative note offsets. The voice adds each read byte to its base note. $80 restarts the sequence at its saved offset.
A negative command updates the current song. A nonnegative command below $7F initializes a song, and $7F returns immediately.

Multiplies the song index by six and copies the three track pointers. Clears the current track and pattern cursors, active frequency and note-duration state and initializes the SID filter. Instrument selection sets the voice effects separately.
Starts the three-voice update at voice index two. Reads the SID register offset indexed by that voice.
When the remaining note duration exceeds one, decrements it and the two secondary effect timers, then continues with the existing note.
Clears the temporary pitch offsets, drops the voice gate and loads the current track pointer. Reads the next pattern number for this voice.
A track byte of $FF resets that voice’s track and pattern offsets and starts reading from the beginning.
The track’s $FE command clears all three SID control registers and sets the command byte to $7F for later ticks.
Combines the indexed low and high pattern pointer bytes and reads the next pattern event. $FF ends the pattern and advances the track position.
Pattern commands at or above $A0 use a two-byte handler table. Patches an absolute jump with that handler and restores the voice index before dispatch.
Low operand byte of the extended-event jump. The pattern decoder writes it from the even bytes of the handler directory.
High operand byte patched by the same dispatcher from the odd bytes of its directory.
A byte from $80 to $9F chooses a nine-byte instrument record. Copies its effect parameters and writes the envelope registers for the current voice.
Finishes installing the voice’s modulation flags, note-stream index, pitch parameters and ADSR bytes. Restores the saved pattern index before reading the next event.
An event from $60 to $7F sets the duration and consumes the next event. Smaller values enter the note trigger.
Converts the note number through the split frequency tables and computes positive and negative effect limits. Writes the instrument control and resets the per-note counters.
Writes the initial SID control byte, copies the configured duration and effect index, and resets the pulse effect state.
Loads the instrument flags and tests bit four when deciding whether to write the follow-up control byte.
After the temporary effect timer expires, adds the positive pitch delta and subtracts the negative pitch delta from the current frequency.
Filter modulation increments or decrements the cutoff high byte. Crossing $30 or $AF reverses the signed step in the immediate operand.
Signed step in the filter sweep’s immediate ADC. The limit branch negates this operand when the cutoff crosses the upper or lower boundary.
Bit zero enables pitch sweep after the effect delay. The direction flag selects a frequency step up or down toward the saved limit.
Bit one enables pulse-width sweep. Reverses the per-voice direction at high bytes $0F and $01.
Bit two enables an upward step of $10 until the frequency high byte reaches $5F.
Bit three enables a downward step while the frequency high byte differs from $01.
Bit four alternates waveform and frequency state between the base note and a second control and frequency value.
Bit five enables a relative note-index sequence. The sequence terminator $80 resets its offset, and each note is read through the frequency tables.
Bit six enables a pulse-width decrement while the corresponding state flag is set. At high byte $08 it clears the flag.
Writes the four frequency and pulse-width registers for the current SID voice. Proceeds with the next voice when one remains.
Writes the shared cutoff high byte, updates the tick countdown and calls the volume decay helper before writing filter mode and master volume.
If the fade request is set, decrements an interval counter until the routine reaches the next volume step.
7 little-endian handler addresses for pattern commands starting at $A0. The player patches the dispatch jump with the selected address.
High-byte read base for the little-endian command addresses. The decoder uses twice the command number as the index.
Reads the next two pattern bytes as a positive frequency adjustment and its effect timer.
Reads the next two pattern bytes as a negative frequency adjustment and its effect timer.
Stores the next pattern byte as the index to restore when the note sequence reaches $80.
Uses the next pattern byte as the following note’s default duration.
Uses the next pattern byte as the voice’s pulse sweep step.
Uses the next pattern byte as the active note countdown. Saves the following pattern offset and continues updating voice effects.
Argument zero sets the filter control and resonance byte to $F0. Argument one enables modulation and writes $F1. Other values clear the stored cutoff.
Low frequency bytes for the 96 note indices. Paired with the high bytes in the next table.
High frequency bytes for the 96 note indices, selected along with their low bytes by the note trigger.
Five six-byte headers with three low and three high track-pointer bytes per song index.
Song 0, voice 1. This track lists 32 pattern indices followed by the loop command $FF.
Song 0, voice 2. This track lists 17 pattern indices followed by the loop command $FF.

Song 4, voice 3. This track lists 1 pattern indices followed by the stop command $FE.
Low bytes for the pattern pointers indexed by each voice’s track byte.
High bytes for those pattern pointers, paired with the low-byte table.

Alternate waveform and gate byte loaded into the current voice’s secondary control state.
Initial pulse width high byte selected for the voice.

Instrument field used to form the frequency modulation limits.

Sets the stack, blanks the screen, clears the working zero page and sets up the bitmap and its colour tables. Reads the side marker at $07F2 and branches to the reset path unless its masked value is S.
Clears the stop byte at $08DA and calls the bitmap reveal at $08DB. Then waits for a key or joystick fire and sets the music request byte at $0C4D.
Selects the KERNAL and I/O with low port bits $06, restores zero page from $C800, hides sprites and disables interrupts before testing the side marker at $07F1.
Blanks the display, clears the working zero page and several state pages, enables the ROMs and jumps to the KERNAL reset routine.
Zero byte between the jump to KERNAL reset and the raster IRQ installer.
Writes the RAM vector for $1945, enables VIC raster interrupts, disables CIA interrupts and schedules the raster comparison at $32.
Acknowledges VIC raster IRQs and schedules line $32. Bumps the interlude tick and calls $0CDB on odd tick values.
Tick incremented by the raster IRQ. Its low bit selects the music-update phase.
Transfers SP to X, reads the stacked status through $0107,X and enters the restart handler if its break bit is set.
Initializes positions and colours for eight text sprites. Installs pointers $40–$47 at $D7F8–$D7FF while I/O is hidden.
Switches to the memory mapping with character ROM visible and zeros the RAM underneath at $D000–$D1FF. Then restores I/O.
Uses the requested line index to choose 24 screen codes. Reads eight bytes per glyph from character ROM, and writes the rows with a stride of three into eight sprite slots in RAM under I/O.
English side A message, “PLEASE TURN TO SIDE A”. Each stored line occupies 24 character positions.
English side B message, “PLEASE TURN TO SIDE B”. Each stored line occupies 24 character positions.
German side A message, “DISKETTENSEITE A”. Each stored line occupies 24 character positions.
German side B message, “DISKETTENSEITE B”. Each stored line occupies 24 character positions.
Italian side A message, “PASSA AL LATO A”. Each stored line occupies 24 character positions.
Italian side B message, “PASSA AL LATO B”. Each stored line occupies 24 character positions.
Offsets at a stride of 24 bytes for the disk messages and the end of the message table.
Eight offsets spaced three bytes apart. The writer uses them to store one byte per glyph row.
Twenty-four little-endian offsets within the eight sprite slots. Each has the column within one of the three-byte sprite rows added to the corresponding slot base.
Sets the low processor-port bits to $03, exposing the character ROM for source reads and RAM for destination writes.
Restores processor-port bits $05 for access to VIC and other I/O registers.
Delays between input scans and returns when the keyboard result is nonzero or either controller has its Fire bit set.
Selects I/O and RAM under the ROMs, copies the cartridge header to $8000 and writes the hardware and software vector bytes.
Two entry words point to $1C0E and precede the five-byte CBM80 signature. The setup loop at $1BDF copies the nine bytes to $8000.
Sets the stack, clears the CIA interrupt enables, banks the ROMs out with I/O visible, and jumps to the start at $1800.
Clears zero-page addresses $02-$FF, preserving the processor port at $00-$01.
Polls the joystick and keyboard until the keyboard decoder reports a code or the combined joystick mask has bit 4 set.
Runs an inner 256-decrement Y loop for each outer decrement of X.
Waits for the low raster byte at $D012 to match X.
Sets the VIC display-enable bit while clearing the high raster-compare bit.
Clears VIC display enable and the high raster-compare bit.
Combined pressed-input bits from both joystick ports. The interlude waits for the Fire bit.
Active-high joystick mask from CIA 1 port A.
Active-high joystick mask from CIA 1 port B.
Result accumulated by the interlude keyboard scan. A nonzero value can advance the illustration.
Keyboard scan column number, counted down from seven through zero.
Reads both CIA 1 joystick inputs as active-low masks and combines their five inverted input bits into $1C6E.
Cycles the eight column masks at $1D01 through CIA 1 port A, reads the rows from port B and ORs the corresponding keycodes into the result. A code of $FF ends the current column scan.
Storage updated at the end of each scan with the decoded keyboard mask.
Eight active-low masks for the CIA keyboard columns. The scan selects a different output bit on each pass.
Eight eight-byte groups of keycodes. The scanner indexes the group for each selected column by the position of a low row bit.
Selects VIC bank $C000, screen matrix $D400 and bitmap $E000. Sets multicolour bitmap mode, sets the border and background to black, and disables sprites.
Clears CHAREN and copies 1016 screen-matrix bytes from $3DE3 to $D400–$D7F7. The last eight matrix bytes hold the separately installed sprite pointers.
Copies the four cell-colour pages into the colour RAM chip. Also copies the bitmap tail page at $3C63 into display RAM at $FE80.
Writes zero to all 32 pages of the bitmap area $E000-$FFFF before drawing the picture.
Stored multicolour bitmap bytes for destination $E000–$E3FF. $091C reveals these pixels in masked passes.
Stored multicolour bitmap bytes for destination $E400–$E7FF. $091C reveals these pixels in masked passes.
Stored multicolour bitmap bytes for destination $E800–$EBFF. $091C reveals these pixels in masked passes.
Stored multicolour bitmap bytes for destination $EC00–$EFFF. $091C reveals these pixels in masked passes.
Stored multicolour bitmap bytes for destination $F000–$F3FF. $091C reveals these pixels in masked passes.
Stored multicolour bitmap bytes for destination $F400–$F7FF. $091C reveals these pixels in masked passes.
Stored multicolour bitmap bytes for destination $F800–$FBFF. $091C reveals these pixels in masked passes.
Stored multicolour bitmap bytes for destination $FC00–$FE7F. $091C reveals these pixels in masked passes.
A page copied to $FE80 while installing the colour RAM. The bitmap reveal also reads part of this source page.
Screen matrix bytes for $D400–$D4FF. The high and low nibbles select the two cell colours for bitmap pixel pairs 01 and 10.
Screen matrix bytes for $D500–$D5FF. The high and low nibbles select the two cell colours for bitmap pixel pairs 01 and 10.
Screen matrix bytes for $D600–$D61C. The high and low nibbles select the two cell colours for bitmap pixel pairs 01 and 10.
Screen matrix bytes for $D61D–$D6F7. The high and low nibbles select the two cell colours for bitmap pixel pairs 01 and 10.
Screen matrix bytes for $D6F8–$D7F7. The high and low nibbles select the two cell colours for bitmap pixel pairs 01 and 10.
Eight repeated bytes at the end of the stored matrix allocation. The matrix copy ends immediately before them. The VIC matrix positions at those offsets hold sprite pointers.
Colour RAM source page for $D800–$D8FF, written by $1DA5. The low nibble selects the colour for multicolour bitmap pixel pair 11.
Colour RAM source page for $D900–$D9FF, written by $1DA5. The low nibble selects the colour for multicolour bitmap pixel pair 11.
Colour RAM source page for $DA00–$DAFF, written by $1DA5. The low nibble selects the colour for multicolour bitmap pixel pair 11.
Colour RAM source page for $DB00–$DBFF, written by $1DA5. The low nibble selects the colour for multicolour bitmap pixel pair 11.
Destination for the nine-byte header at $1C05. Both vector words in the installed header point to the interlude restart entry.
Page of mutable game state cleared on the interlude failure exit.
Shared progress and high-score page. The reset clears it and the loading display reads the language field within it.
Language number used to choose the corresponding loading-script address.
RAM NMI and reset vectors point to $1C0E during the picture. The hardware IRQ vector points to the raster service at $1945.
